analysis.one_liner: Bars data brokers from selling personal data for stalking, fraud, or discrimination, and makes them register with the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with both a Democrat and two Republicans behind it, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets companies that collect personal information about people they have no direct relationship with and sell it to other businesses. It would ban data brokers from getting personal information through fraud, from selling it to buyers they should know plan to use it for stalking, identity theft, or discrimination, and would require them to maintain security programs against breaches. It would also force every data broker to register with the Federal Trade Commission each year, with the registry published online so people can see who is selling their data and how to opt out, and it lets the FTC enforce the rules like any other unfair business practice [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose personal information is bought and sold without their knowledge. A public FTC registry would show people which companies hold and sell their data and how to opt out, and the bill targets the uses of that data that cause the most direct harm: stalking, identity theft, financial fraud, and discrimination in employment, housing, and credit [S3]. It would particularly help victims of domestic violence and stalking, whose whereabouts are often located through brokered data [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data is sold by brokers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits data brokers from acquiring personal information by fraudulent means and from using it for stalking or harassment, fraud including identity theft, or unlawful discrimination in employment, housing, and credit decisions [S3].

Bars brokers from selling personal data to a third party they know or reasonably should know intends to use it for those prohibited purposes, and requires security programs and breach counts disclosed at registration [S3].

Requires every data broker to register annually with the FTC, disclose what data it collects, its opt-out methods and their limits, and the number of breaches it suffered, with the registry posted publicly on the FTC website [S3].

Makes violations enforceable by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices, with civil penalties for failing to register, and requires an annual FTC report to Congress on compliance and enforcement [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the businesses that buy their data. Brokers would bear the cost of security programs, annual registration, and exposure of their practices in a public registry, and would face FTC enforcement and penalties; the resale market for personal data would shrink where prohibited uses are involved [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and the data resale market

drawbacks.text: The bill does not give consumers a right to delete their data or opt out of all sales; it only requires brokers to disclose where opt-outs exist and to explain where they do not, so most data trading could continue legally [S3].
Enforcement runs only through the FTC; there is no private right of action letting individuals sue a broker that sold their data to a stalker, so victims depend on agency action [S3].

Broad exclusions shrink coverage: data regulated under other laws (credit reports, banking, health), identity-verification and fraud-prevention uses, publicly available information, and consumer-directed sharing are all carved out, and the definition exempts businesses the consumer has a recent direct relationship with [S3].
Annual registration and security programs create compliance costs that fall hardest on smaller brokers, though the rules are scaled to a firm's size and resources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a transparency-and-enforcement measure, not a comprehensive data rights law. It would deliver real, targeted protection where brokered data causes concrete harm to people, and the public registry would give consumers their first clear window into an industry that operates invisibly. But it leaves the underlying business of data brokering largely intact and relies entirely on FTC enforcement. The main cost of the bill not passing falls on consumers, who remain unable to see who is selling their information or hold brokers accountable through any means other than FTC cases under existing law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2021 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Gary Peters introduced the Data Broker List Act of 2021 on June 24, 2021, together with Sens. Cynthia Lummis and Shelley Moore Capito [S1] [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote followed; the bill's complete action history ends at the committee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the companies that buy their data, who face no new registration, disclosure, or prohibited-use rules; consumers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers, whose industry stays unregistered

for.name: Sen. Gary Peters
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Cynthia Lummis and Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Maria Cantwell (D-WA) never scheduled the bill for action
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan, a Democrat leading with two Republican cosponsors, but no vote was ever taken so the chamber's parties never took a position on record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Companies selling personal information on people they have no relationship with would face fraud-acquisition bans, prohibited-use bans, security duties, annual public FTC registration, and civil penalties. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against consumers' interest in knowing and limiting how their data is traded [S3].

industries.industry: Advertising, marketing, and analytics firms that buy consumer data
industries.note: Buyers of brokered data would lose access to information sold for prohibited purposes like stalking or discrimination, but routine marketing data flows would largely continue since the bill leaves the core business intact [S3].
